```{r setup}
library(dplyr); library(knitr); library(here)
t1 <- read.csv(here("output", "table1_dynamic.csv"),   check.names = FALSE)
t2 <- read.csv(here("output", "table2_onset.csv"),     check.names = FALSE)
t3 <- read.csv(here("output", "table3_canonical.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
```

# TL;DR

Across ~100 model cells (four regime-event codings x three control generations x
two estimators, all with method-of-composition uncertainty propagation over 900
posterior draws), the results form a **mirror asymmetry**:

> **Public discontent destabilizes autocracies; public support stabilizes
> democracies; neither works the other way around.** Discontent among
> autocratic publics precedes both the *onset* of regime-change episodes and
> *completed democratization* (DD and BMR codings). Support among democratic
> publics lowers the hazard that erosion episodes *begin*. Discontent never
> predicts democratic breakdown under any operationalization, and support never
> protects autocracies.

This is the sentence the theory, introduction, and conclusion should be built
around.

# Design in one paragraph

IV = DCPO latent political discontent (PPD; 900 posterior draws) and Claassen-style
democratic support, both on 0--100 scales. Every model is estimated twice: once
on posterior-mean data ("naive") and once by the method of composition over the
900 draws (Tai--Hu--Solt), so every table displays how naive significance
attenuates once measurement uncertainty is honored. Timing is a uniform
one-year opinion-precedes-outcome gap throughout (lagged IVs in the dynamic
panel; lead-coded events with current-year covariates for boundary cells;
episode-onset cells lag the full RHS). Event DVs come from four codings --
V-Dem ERT episodes/Regimes-of-the-World boundaries, DD (Bjornskov--Rode update),
Boix--Miller--Rosato, and Geddes--Wright--Frantz (supplementary; ends 2010) --
each with its own duration clock and transition-history control. Hazards are
discrete-time logits estimated by both plain (clustered) and Firth penalized
likelihood; the dynamic panel follows Claassen 2020 (pooled OLS + system GMM).

# Main results

## Table 1 -- opinion does not move annual democracy levels

```{r}
kable(t1, align = "llrrrrrr")
```

Everything is null under the full specification once MOC is applied (support's
naive significance attenuates away -- the Tai-pattern replication). This is the
set-up result: the Claassen-style *level-change* design finds nothing, which
motivates moving to discrete regime events.

## Table 2 -- the 2x2: onset of regime-change episodes

```{r}
kable(t2, align = "lllrrrrrr")
```

Panel A is the paper's core. Within one pooled hazard (shared baseline and
controls, opinion slopes split by regime type at t-1):

- **Discontent, autocratic public: positive, MOC p = .011/.023** -- discontent
  precedes episode onset in autocracies.
- **Support, democratic public: negative (protective), MOC p = .012/.015.**
- Both cross-terms are null (.50--.66).
- Formal asymmetry tests (draw-wise slope differences): support asymmetry
  significant (~.04), discontent asymmetry marginal (~.07).

Panels B--C are direction-specific onsets: liberalization onset in autocracies is
directionally positive but underpowered (18 events); erosion onset in
democracies shows *no* discontent effect (the doom narrative fails even at the
process-start stage) while support remains protective.

## Table 3 -- completed transitions across canonical codings

```{r}
kable(t3, align = "lllrrrrrr")
```

The same split-IV design on each coding's own democracy boundary: the
autocratic-public discontent slope (= democratization side) survives MOC in
**DD (.036/.039)** and **BMR (.011/.012)**; the democratic-public slope
(= breakdown side) is null everywhere. The within-coding asymmetry test is
significant in all four BMR cells (p = .011--.038) and marginal in DD. GWF (16
events, coverage ends 2010) is null and flagged exploratory.

# What we CAN claim

1. **Discontent precedes the start of regime-change processes**, and this is
   concentrated among autocratic publics (Table 2A).
2. **Discontent precedes completed democratization** under turnover-based
   dichotomous codings (DD, BMR), with the democratization-vs-breakdown
   asymmetry formally significant in BMR.
3. **Support protects democracies at the episode-onset stage** (additive main
   effect).
4. **Discontent does not predict democratic breakdown under any of the four
   codings**, nor erosion-episode onset -- a strong, multiply-operationalized
   null that speaks directly against the "discontent kills democracy"
   narrative.
5. **Naive analysis overstates certainty**: many naive-significant cells die
   under MOC; the paper's surviving claims are exactly those robust to
   measurement uncertainty.

# What we must NOT claim (framing guardrails)

- **No buffering / "critical citizens" conditional claims.** Support's
  protection is an *additive* main effect. The discontent-x-support interaction
  was tested throughout (dynamic panel and hazards): directionally consistent,
  uniformly null under MOC. Do not write "support protects democracies *even
  when discontent is high*" or "support conditions the effect of discontent."
- **"Precedes democratization," not "causes democratization."** Observational,
  1-year-lead evidence; elite bargaining, international factors, etc. intervene
  between onset and completion (the ERT completion cells are null -- discontent
  knocks on the door; other forces open it).
- **The completion result is coding-conditional.** It appears in the
  turnover-based dichotomies (DD, BMR), not in ERT's index-threshold crossings
  or GWF's regime cases. This is not a contradiction: an event-overlap audit
  shows the three "democratization" DVs share only ~25--35% of their events
  (appendix table). State which definitions carry the result.
- **Do not cite the pooled onset(all) cell as the headline.** It sits in a
  borderline band (MOC p .04--.05 across reruns) because it pools the strong
  autocratic signal with the null democratic one; the split-IV cell (Table 2A)
  is the main evidence.
- **GWF cells and the liberalization-onset cell are exploratory** (5--18
  events). Regime-split GMM does not exist (singular under the full
  specification) -- mention only in the appendix.
- Small-event caveats and multiple-comparisons language should stay in the
  results section; the surviving claims cluster coherently (onset + completion,
  same direction, multiple codings), which is the honest defense.

# Pointers for each section

- **Theory/framing**: the organizing idea is that mass opinion erodes the
  *status-quo regime*, with regime-type-asymmetric consequences: Welzel-style
  aspirations push autocracies toward democracy; Easton/Claassen-style diffuse
  support keeps democracies from starting to erode. The two null cells are
  theoretically load-bearing: discontent does not kill democracies (contra
  Foa/Mounk), and popular support does not save autocracies.
- **Literature**: `paper/lit_review_regime_stability.md` is complete and
  web-verified: no opinion-IV study uses event DVs; none of the 18 canonical
  stability-DV studies includes mass opinion. The gap paragraph writes itself
  from its Part 1/Part 3 tables.
- **Introduction**: lead with the doom narrative (discontent as threat to
  democracy), report that the threat is real but points the other way -- at
  autocracies.
- **Conclusion**: measurement matters twice -- (i) uncertainty propagation
  (naive vs MOC), (ii) event definitions (the overlap audit). Both are
  portable lessons beyond this paper.
- **Data/Methods and Results**: JC is drafting; all numbers in this memo come
  from `output/results_main_combined.csv` and the table generator
  `codes/final_02_tables_main.R` (rerun-safe, reads saved results only).

# Significance markers

`+` p < .10, `**` p < .05, `***` p < .01 (two-sided). MOC estimates are means of
900 draw-level coefficient draws; MOC standard errors are the draw standard
deviations (total uncertainty: sampling + measurement).
